name: Archias of Mytilene
bio: Archias of Mytilene is one of the epigrammatists whose short poems were gathered in the Greek Anthology. Paton's index of authors records the poet's date as unknown. Paton's index lists the poet among the writers of the Wreath of Philippus, with a query.
This archive carries the 3 epigrams ascribed to the poet in the third volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Book IX: 19, 111, 339).

poems.title: Book IX, 19
poems.author: Archias of Mytilene
poems.text: “Race,” who once outshone all fleet-footed horses; about whose legs chaplets once hung; he whom Pytho, the oracular seat of Phoebus, once crowned in the games, where he raced like a swiftly flying bird; he whom Nemea, too, the nurse of the grim lion, crowned, and Pisa and Isthmus with its two beaches, is now fettered by a collar as if by a bit, and grinds corn by turning arough stone. He suffers the same fate as Heracles, who also, after accomplishing so much, put on the yoke of slavery.

poems.title: Book IX, 111
poems.author: Archias of Mytilene
poems.text: We should praise the Thracians because they mourn for their children when they issue from their mothers’ wombs to the light, while on the other hand they bless those on whom Death, the unforeseen servant of the Fates, lays his hand. For the living ever pass through every kind of evil, but the dead have found the medicine of all.

poems.title: Book IX, 339
poems.author: Archias of Mytilene
poems.text: A raven plying his black wings in the pellucid sky, saw once a scorpion emerging from the ground, and swooped down to catch it; but the scorpion, as the raven dashed down to the ground, was not slow to strike his foot with its powerful sting, and robbed him of life. See how the luckless bird met with the fate he was preparing for another by means of that other.
